A famine in North Korea in the mid 1990s, which the government called the "Arduous March". Estimates of the dead vary widely; most scholars put them in the hundreds of thousands, and some go above two million.

North Korea's farms depended on Soviet fuel, fertiliser and cheap trade. When the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, that help ended, and China cut its aid too. Floods in 1995 and 1996 and drought in 1997 ruined harvests. The state ration system, which fed most people, broke down. Kim Il Sung died in 1994, and his son Kim Jong Il put the army first.

People survived by foraging, by trading in markets the state had banned, and by crossing into China. Those private markets never went away, and they changed how North Koreans live. Foreign food aid came from the late 1990s. It was one of the worst famines of the late twentieth century, in the northern half of divided Korea.
sum: A famine in North Korea in the mid 1990s, which the government called the "Arduous March". Estimates of the dead vary widely; most scholars put them in the hundreds of thousands, and some go above two million.
